# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.
----
# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

Source: project wiki benchmark, March 2026 (sources/ostrich-benchmark-2026.md)."

final.result:
**Probably not, and nothing in `./sources` shows that it is.**

- **Wrong kind of data:** The README says Ostrich is a dictionary compressor "for small text records". Your archives are protobuf-encoded binary frames, 40–300 MB per file.
- **The benchmark doesn't cover your case:** The 4.1× ratio (against 3.2× for zstd level 3) at 410 MB/s came from text log files under 1 MB. The benchmark itself says binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs were not tested, so it tells you nothing about your workload.
- **Extra work:** Ostrich trains a dictionary per stream and needs that same dictionary to decompress. You'd have to store and version the dictionaries alongside the archives.

To decide properly, run Ostrich and zstd (and maybe xz) on a few real nightly files and compare ratio and speed. Until then, I'd stick with zstd.

I also saved both source findings to the research memory for later sessions.
